summaryBox.title: Gas-Phase Kinetics
summaryBox.takeaway: For A(g) ──► B(g) + C(g): P_A = 2P₀ - P_t. k = (2.303/t) log₁₀(P₀ / (2P₀ - P_t)).

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
GAS-PHASE FIRST-ORDER DERIVATION

Consider a first-order gas-phase reaction: A(g) ──► B(g) + C(g)
Let P₀ be the initial pressure of A(g), and P_t be the total pressure at time t:

Reaction:          A(g) ──► B(g) + C(g)
Initial (t=0):     P₀        0      0
At Time t:         P₀ - x    x      x

P_t = (P₀ - x) + x + x = P₀ + x  ⟹  x = P_t - P₀
P_A = P₀ - x = P₀ - (P_t - P₀) = 2P₀ - P_t

k = (2.303 / t) log₁₀ [ P₀ / (2P₀ - P_t) ]
conceptBreakdown.content:
Consider a first-order gas-phase reaction: $A(g) \longrightarrow B(g) + C(g)$. Let $P_0$ be the initial pressure of $A(g)$, and $P_t$ be the total pressure at time $t$:
$$\text{Reaction: } A(g) \longrightarrow B(g) + C(g)$$
$$\text{Initial } (t=0): P_0 \quad \quad 0 \quad \quad 0$$
$$\text{At Time } t: P_0 - x \quad \quad x \quad \quad x$$

$$P_t = (P_0 - x) + x + x = P_0 + x \implies x = P_t - P_0$$
$$P_A = P_0 - x = P_0 - (P_t - P_0) = 2P_0 - P_t$$

$$\mathbf{k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_0}{2P_0 - P_t} \right)}$$

conceptBreakdown.heading: 5.2 Pseudo-First-Order Reactions
conceptBreakdown.title: 5.2 Pseudo-First-Order Reactions
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
PSEUDO-FIRST-ORDER REACTIONS

A reaction that is inherently higher-order (e.g., second-order) but behaves kinetic-wise as a first-order reaction because one of the reactants is present in large excess, rendering its concentration practically constant.

Inversion of Cane Sugar:
  C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O (Excess) ──[H⁺]──► C₆H₁₂O₆ (Glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (Fructose)

Actual Rate Law = k' [C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁] [H₂O]
Since [H₂O] ≈ Constant ⟹ Rate = k [C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁]  where k = k' [H₂O]

Pseudo-First-Order Rate Constant:
  k = (2.303 / t) log₁₀ [ (r₀ - r_∞) / (r_t - r_∞) ]
where r₀, r_t, r_∞ are optical rotation angles measured using a polarimeter.
conceptBreakdown.content:
A reaction that is inherently higher-order (e.g., second-order) but behaves kinetic-wise as a first-order reaction because one of the reactants is present in large excess, rendering its concentration practically constant.

$$\text{Inversion of Cane Sugar: } \text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (Excess)} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$
$$\text{Actual Rate Law} = k' [\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}] [\text{H}_2\text{O}]$$
$$\text{Since } [\text{H}_2\text{O}] \approx \text{Constant} \implies \mathbf{\text{Rate} = k [\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}] \quad \text{where } k = k' [\text{H}_2\text{O}]}$$

$$\mathbf{k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log_{10} \left( \frac{r_0 - r_\infty}{r_t - r_\infty} \right)}$$
where $r_0, r_t, r_\infty$ are optical rotation angles measured using a polarimeter.

quickRevision: A(g) ──► 2B(g) + C(g): P_t = P₀ + 2x ⟹ P_A = P₀ - (P_t - P₀)/2.
Sugar inversion and acid ester hydrolysis are pseudo-first-order.
Sugar inversion rate constant: k = (2.303/t) log₁₀((r₀ - r_∞)/(r_t - r_∞)).
Alkaline saponification is a true second-order reaction.
